title: Clustering
description: Finding groups without labels: k-means, hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering and how to judge a clustering.
overview: In unsupervised learning there are no labels to predict. The data are only inputs x^{(1)}, …, x^{(m)}, and the task is to find structure in them. The most common structure is a division into groups of similar points. Marketers cluster customers, biologists cluster genes and cells, and search engines cluster documents.

There is no single right answer, since what counts as a cluster depends on the notion of similarity and on the purpose. This chapter presents the three main families (centroid-based, hierarchical and density-based), shows when each fails, and discusses how to evaluate a result that has no ground truth.
objectives: Write the k-means objective and run Lloyd's algorithm by hand.
Prove that k-means converges, and explain why it only finds a local minimum.
Choose k with the elbow method and the silhouette score.
Build a dendrogram with single, complete and average linkage.
Describe DBSCAN and decide which clustering method suits a data set.

sections.title: k-means
body: Imagine placing k post offices in a town so that every house is close to its nearest one. You can do it by trial: guess locations, send each house to its nearest post office, then move each post office to the middle of the houses it serves. Moving changes which house is nearest to which office, so repeat until nothing changes. That is k-means. **k-means** partitions m points into k clusters, each represented by its mean, the **centroid** μ_j. It minimizes the **within-cluster sum of squares** (the inertia):

where c^{(i)} ∈ {1, …, k} is the cluster assigned to point i. Minimizing over both the assignments and the centroids at once is NP-hard, but alternating between the two is easy, because each is simple with the other held fixed. **Lloyd's algorithm**:

list: Initialize the centroids μ₁, …, μ_k (for example, k random data points).
**Assignment step**: assign each point to its nearest centroid, c^{(i)} = argmin_j ‖x^{(i)} − μ_j‖².
**Update step**: move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points, μ_j = (1/|C_j|) Σ_{i ∈ C_j} x^{(i)}.
Repeat until the assignments stop changing.

body.key: Each step cannot increase J. The assignment step picks the best c for fixed μ. The update step picks the best μ for fixed c: the mean minimizes the sum of squared distances to a set of points. J is bounded below by 0 and there are finitely many partitions, so the algorithm converges in finitely many steps, to a local minimum (not necessarily the global one).

example.title: k-means on six points
example.problem: The data are 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12 and k = 2. Start with centroids 2 and 3. Run the algorithm to convergence and report J.
solution: **Assign**: 1 and 2 are nearer to 2, and 3, 10, 11, 12 are nearer to 3. Clusters {1, 2} and {3, 10, 11, 12}.
**Assign**: now 3 is nearer to 1.5 (distance 1.5) than to 9 (distance 6). Clusters {1, 2, 3} and {10, 11, 12}.
**Update**: μ₁ = 2, μ₂ = 11. J = (1 + 0 + 1) + (1 + 0 + 1) = 4. The next assignment changes nothing, so the algorithm stops. J fell from 50.5 to 4.

list: **Initialization**: poor starting centroids give poor local minima. Run the algorithm several times from different starts and keep the lowest J. **k-means++** picks the first centroid at random and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centroid already chosen, which spreads the starts out and carries a provable guarantee on the expected cost (within a factor of O(log k) of optimal).
**Cost**: each iteration takes O(mkn) time for n features, which scales to millions of points.
**Scale**: use standardized features, because the distance is dominated by large-range features.

**Assumptions**: k-means finds compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size, since it uses Euclidean distance to a mean. It fails on elongated or ring-shaped clusters, and is sensitive to outliers (use k-medoids, which uses an actual data point as the center, to be robust).
**Hard assignment**: each point belongs to exactly one cluster. The next chapter's Gaussian mixture gives soft assignments, and k-means is its limiting case.

check.a: Each step does not increase the objective, which is bounded below, and there are finitely many partitions

sections.title: Choosing the number of clusters
body: The number of clusters k is a hyperparameter, and J always decreases as k increases (at k = m, J = 0), so J alone cannot choose it.

Plot the optimal J against k. Adding clusters helps a lot until the true structure is captured and then yields only small gains, so the curve bends at an 'elbow'. The bend is often ambiguous in real data.

body: For a point i, let a(i) be the average distance to the other points in its own cluster, and b(i) the smallest average distance to the points of any other cluster. The **silhouette** is
It is near +1 when a point sits well inside its cluster, near 0 on a boundary, and negative when it is probably in the wrong cluster. The average silhouette over all points is maximized to choose k.

example.title: A silhouette value
example.problem: A point has an average distance of 1.0 to its own cluster mates and an average distance of 4.0 to the nearest other cluster. Find its silhouette.

list: **External** measures compare a clustering with known labels when they exist, such as the adjusted Rand index (1 for perfect agreement, about 0 for random) and normalized mutual information.
**Stability**: cluster resampled versions of the data and check that the groups persist.
**Usefulness**: ultimately, ask whether the clusters make sense to a domain expert and serve the purpose, for example marketing segments that lead to different actions.

wrong: J is undefined for k > 2
J increases with k

sections.title: Hierarchical clustering
body: Hierarchical clustering produces a tree of nested clusters instead of a single partition, so k need not be chosen in advance. **Agglomerative** clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until only one remains. The record of merges, drawn as a tree with the merge distance as the height, is a **dendrogram**. Cutting the tree at a chosen height gives a flat clustering.
The result depends on the **linkage**, the definition of the distance between two clusters A and B:

eqs: single: d(A, B) = min d(a, b)
nearest members; can chain clusters together through a bridge of points
complete: d(A, B) = max d(a, b)
farthest members; compact clusters of similar diameter
average: d(A, B) = mean d(a, b)
Ward: merge the pair that least increases total within-cluster variance

example.title: Single versus complete linkage
example.problem: Points on a line at 1, 2, 6, 7 and 15. Build the dendrogram with single and with complete linkage.
solution: In both methods, {1, 2} merges at height 1 and {6, 7} merges at height 1.
**Single**: the distance between {1, 2} and {6, 7} is min = 6 − 2 = 4, so they merge at 4. Then 15 joins at 15 − 7 = 8.
**Complete**: the distance between {1, 2} and {6, 7} is max = 7 − 1 = 6, so they merge at 6. Then 15 joins at 15 − 1 = 14.
The merge order is the same here, but the heights differ, and on larger data sets the cluster shapes would differ too: single linkage forms long chains, complete linkage forms tight groups.

body: The naive algorithm costs O(m³) time (O(m² log m) with a priority queue) and O(m²) memory, so it suits thousands, not millions, of points. Its strength is the dendrogram, which shows the structure at every scale and is the standard display in genomics and taxonomy.

check.q: Which linkage can chain together long, thin clusters through a line of intermediate points?
wrong: Complete linkage
Ward's method
None of them

sections.title: Density-based and spectral clustering
body: k-means and Ward's method find round blobs. A cluster can instead be defined as a region of high density separated from other regions by low density, which may have any shape.

**DBSCAN** has two parameters: a radius ε and a count minPts. A point is a **core point** if at least minPts points (itself included) lie within distance ε. Core points within ε of each other are linked into one cluster. A non-core point within ε of a core point joins that cluster as a border point. All remaining points are **noise**.

list: It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, determines the number of clusters itself, and labels outliers explicitly.
It struggles when clusters have very different densities, since one ε cannot fit them all, and in high dimensions, where distances concentrate (see the Curse of Dimensionality).
A common choice of ε comes from the 'knee' in the sorted distances to the minPts-th neighbor.

body: **Spectral clustering** treats the data as a graph with edge weights W_ij = exp(−‖x_i − x_j‖²/(2σ²)), and cuts the graph into pieces with few strong edges between them. The graph Laplacian is L = D − W, where D is the diagonal matrix of row sums of W. The eigenvectors of L with the smallest eigenvalues give a low-dimensional embedding in which the clusters become compact, and k-means is then run on this embedding. The number of zero eigenvalues of L equals the number of connected components of the graph.

Spectral clustering handles ring-shaped and intertwined clusters that defeat k-means, at the cost of an eigendecomposition of an m × m matrix (O(m³) naively; sparse and approximate methods scale further).

check.q: In DBSCAN, a point that has fewer than minPts neighbors within ε and is not near a core point is
wrong: a new cluster
a centroid
assigned to the nearest cluster

quiz.q: The points 0, 4, 6, 10 are clustered with k = 2 and initial centroids 0 and 10. After one assignment step and one update step, the centroids are
wrong: 0 and 10, unchanged
5 and 5
quiz.why: Point 4 is nearer to 0 and point 6 is nearer to 10, so the clusters are {0, 4} and {6, 10} with means 2 and 8. The option 3.33 and 10 wrongly sends 6 to the first centroid.

quiz.q: A k-means clustering has clusters {2, 4} and {9, 13}, each with its centroid at the mean. What is the within-cluster sum of squares J?
quiz.why: The means are 3 and 11. The squared deviations are 1, 1, 4 and 4, which sum to 10. The value 6 adds absolute deviations, and 2.5 is the mean rather than the sum.

quiz.q: Which claim about k-means is false?
quiz.a: With k-means++ initialization the algorithm is guaranteed to reach the global minimum of J
wrong: Lloyd's algorithm never increases J from one iteration to the next
Different random starts can end at different final clusterings
The cost of one iteration grows linearly with the number of points
quiz.why: k-means++ gives a bound on the expected cost (within O(log k) of optimal), not a guarantee of the global minimum. Lloyd's algorithm only reaches a local minimum.

quiz.q: Customers are described by yearly income in dollars (0 to 200,000) and age in years (20 to 80). k-means is run on the raw values. What is the likely result?
quiz.a: The clusters are determined almost entirely by income
wrong: The clusters are determined almost entirely by age
Both features count equally, since the update step uses means
The algorithm fails to converge because of the different units
quiz.why: Euclidean distance is dominated by the feature with the largest range. Standardizing the features first gives each a comparable influence.

quiz.q: A few extreme outliers pull k-means centroids away from the bulk of the data. Which change makes the cluster centers robust to them?
quiz.a: Use k-medoids, where each center is an actual data point
wrong: Use more iterations of Lloyd's algorithm
Replace squared distance by squared distance to the origin
Initialize with k-means++ instead of random points
quiz.why: A mean is moved by any single extreme value. A medoid is a data point chosen from the cluster, so a distant outlier shifts it far less. More iterations and better initialization do not change what the center is.

quiz.q: In k-means++, the next centroid is chosen from the data points with probability proportional to
quiz.a: its squared distance to the nearest centroid already chosen
wrong: its distance to the nearest centroid already chosen, not squared
the same value for every point
the number of points within ε of it
quiz.why: Squared distance favors points far from the existing centroids, which spreads the starting centroids out. Uniform choice is ordinary random initialization.

quiz.q: The best J for k = 1 to 6 is 900, 400, 150, 130, 120, 115. Which k does the elbow method suggest?
quiz.why: The drops are 500, 250, 20, 10, 5. J falls sharply until k = 3 and only slowly afterward, so the bend is at 3. The smallest J is at k = 6, but J always falls as k grows.

quiz.q: A point has an average distance 2.5 to the other points in its own cluster and 5 to the nearest other cluster. Its silhouette is
quiz.why: s = (b − a)/max(a, b) = (5 − 2.5)/5 = 0.5. The value 2.5 omits the division, and −0.5 reverses the sign of b − a.

quiz.q: A point has a silhouette very close to 0. Where is it most likely to be?
quiz.a: On the boundary, about as far from its own cluster as from the nearest other one
wrong: At the centroid of its cluster
Far from every cluster, as an outlier
Inside the wrong cluster, deep in its interior
quiz.why: s = 0 means a(i) = b(i): the average distances to its own cluster and the neighboring cluster are equal. A clearly misassigned point would have a negative value.

quiz.q: A clustering is compared with known class labels, and the adjusted Rand index is about 0.01. The right reading is that
quiz.a: the agreement is about what random cluster assignments would give
wrong: the clusters match the classes but their numbers are permuted
the clusters are compact but too numerous
the classes are balanced, so the index cannot be larger
quiz.why: The adjusted Rand index is 1 for perfect agreement and about 0 for chance agreement. It does not depend on how clusters are numbered, so a permutation alone cannot lower it.

quiz.q: Single linkage is run on points at 0, 3, 5 and 12 on a line. The three merge heights, in order, are
quiz.why: {3, 5} merges at 2. Then 0 joins at its nearest member, 3 − 0 = 3. Then 12 joins at 12 − 5 = 7. The sequence 2, 5, 12 is what complete linkage gives.

quiz.q: A dendrogram of 5 points has merges at heights 1, 2, 6 and 20. If it is cut at height 4, how many clusters result?
quiz.why: Two merges happen below height 4, and each merge reduces the number of clusters by one: 5 − 2 = 3.

quiz.q: Why is naive agglomerative clustering a poor choice for 2 million points?
quiz.a: It needs memory for all pairwise distances, O(m²), and a very large amount of time
wrong: It requires k to be fixed before the algorithm starts
It cannot be used with Euclidean distances
A dendrogram can only be drawn for a few hundred points
quiz.why: The distance matrix has m² entries and the naive algorithm takes O(m³) time. The method does not need k in advance, and it works with many distance measures.

quiz.q: In DBSCAN with minPts = 4, a point has exactly 3 other points within distance ε. The point is
wrong: a border point
a noise point
a centroid
quiz.why: The count includes the point itself, so 3 neighbors plus itself gives 4 = minPts, which makes it a core point.

quiz.q: DBSCAN performs badly on data with one very dense cluster and one very sparse cluster because
quiz.a: a single ε and minPts cannot suit both densities
wrong: it can only find clusters with a spherical shape
it needs to be told the number of clusters
its result depends on the order of the points in the first iteration
quiz.why: An ε small enough to separate the dense regions marks the sparse cluster as noise, while an ε large enough for the sparse cluster merges other structure. DBSCAN finds arbitrary shapes and sets the cluster count itself.

quiz.q: A similarity graph consists of 4 groups of points with no edges between groups. How many zero eigenvalues does its Laplacian L = D − W have?
quiz.why: The number of zero eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian equals the number of connected components, here 4.

quiz.q: In spectral clustering, after the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of the Laplacian are computed, the final step is to
quiz.a: run k-means on the rows of the eigenvector matrix
wrong: take the eigenvectors as the cluster centroids
assign each point to the eigenvector in which it has the largest entry
repeat the graph construction with a smaller σ
quiz.why: The eigenvectors give each point a low-dimensional embedding in which clusters are compact, so k-means then separates them.

quiz.q: A 2-dimensional set of 500,000 points has an unknown number of arbitrarily shaped groups plus scattered outliers. Which method is the best fit?
wrong: k-means, which handles outliers well
complete-linkage hierarchical clustering
spectral clustering with an m × m similarity matrix
quiz.why: DBSCAN finds any shape, chooses the number of clusters itself, labels outliers as noise and scales to large low-dimensional data. k-means assumes round clusters and needs k, and the other two need O(m²) memory or worse.

summary: Clustering groups unlabeled points. k-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares by alternating assignment to the nearest centroid and recomputing the centroids as means.
k-means always converges, but to a local minimum. Use several random starts or k-means++. It assumes round, similar-sized clusters and needs scaled features.
Choose k with the elbow of J(k), the silhouette score, stability and the purpose of the analysis.
Agglomerative clustering merges the closest clusters and yields a dendrogram. Single linkage chains, complete linkage makes compact groups, and Ward's method resembles k-means.
DBSCAN finds dense regions of any shape and marks noise. Spectral clustering uses graph Laplacian eigenvectors to separate non-convex clusters.

problems.q: Run one iteration of k-means on the points 0, 2, 3, 9, 10 with k = 2 and initial centroids 0 and 10. Give the assignments, new centroids and J.
problems.solution: Assignment: 0 and 2 go to centroid 0 (3 is at distance 3 from 0 and 7 from 10, so also to 0); 9 and 10 go to 10. Clusters {0, 2, 3} and {9, 10}. New centroids: 5/3 = 1.667 and 9.5. J = (1.667² + 0.333² + 1.333²) + (0.25 + 0.25) = (2.778 + 0.111 + 1.778) + 0.5 = 5.17.

problems.q: A point has a(i) = 2.0 and b(i) = 1.5. Compute its silhouette and interpret it.
problems.solution: s = (1.5 − 2.0)/max(2.0, 1.5) = −0.5/2 = −0.25. A negative value means the point is closer, on average, to another cluster than to its own: it is probably misassigned.
problems.a: s = −0.25; likely in the wrong cluster.

problems.q: Points on a line: 0, 1, 4, 5, 11. Using complete linkage, give the merge sequence and heights.
problems.solution: {0, 1} at 1 and {4, 5} at 1 (these tie). Then the distance between {0, 1} and {4, 5} is max = 5 − 0 = 5; between {4, 5} and 11 it is 11 − 4 = 7; between {0, 1} and 11 it is 11. So {0, 1} and {4, 5} merge at 5. Then 11 joins at 11 − 0 = 11.

problems.q: Show that for a fixed cluster of points the centroid (the mean) minimizes the sum of squared distances.
problems.solution: Let f(μ) = Σ ‖x_i − μ‖². The gradient is −2 Σ (x_i − μ). Setting it to zero gives μ = (1/N) Σ x_i. The Hessian is 2N I, positive definite, so this is the unique minimum.

problems.q: k-means with k = 2 is run on data from a ring of radius 5 around a dense blob at the center. Predict what happens, and name a method that can separate them.
problems.solution: Both groups have the same center, so no line through two centroids separates them. k-means cuts the data by a line, mixing parts of the ring with the blob. DBSCAN or spectral clustering, which follow density or connectivity, can separate the blob from the ring.
problems.a: k-means splits the data with a straight line and fails; use DBSCAN or spectral clustering.
